title: Tensor Network Solvers for Ultra-large Tight-binding Hamiltonians: Algorithms and Applications
authors: Tiago V. C. Antão, Anouar Moustaj, Yitao Sun, Jose L. Lado
abstract: Understanding quantum materials at meso and even macroscopic scales requires tight-binding calculations on system sizes where explicit matrix representations become prohibitively costly. This represents a major bottleneck to rationalize phenomena in moiré and super-moiré heterostructures and quasicrystals. Here, we present a unified tensor-network methodology to solve tight-binding problems at exceptionally large scales, by mapping a system of $N = 2^L$ sites onto a many-body problem of $L$ pseudospin sites, which is subsequently solved with tensor network algorithms. For Hamiltonians with compressible real-space structure, the tensor network bond dimension remains modest, typically of order a few tens, independent of $N$.Tensor network representations of arbitrary hopping functions including long-range, spatially modulated, and twisted-layer couplings are built with quantics tensor cross interpolation, and all physical observables are evaluated entirely with tensor network algebra without explicit matrix storage or diagonalization. We demonstrate applications to spectral functions, momentum-space spectra via the tensor-network quantum Fourier transform, real-space topological invariants, real-time dynamics, correlation induced symmetry breaking with self-consistent mean-field calculations, non-Hermitian phenomena, and excitonic many-body physics. Our methodology enables routinely solving systems with billions of sites, by leveraging the tensor network compressibility of real-space structures, and establishing a flexible framework to study quantum matter at ultra-large length scales. The methodology is implemented in the open-source Julia package TensorBinding.jl.
summary: The paper introduces a unified tensor-network methodology to solve tight-binding Hamiltonians on ultra-large systems, enabling simulations up to billions of sites. By mapping real-space problems onto MPO representations, it efficiently calculates key observables like spectral functions and topological invariants without storing massive matrices. This breakthrough allows for the study of complex quantum matter in regimes previously inaccessible due to computational cost.
main_problem: Developing scalable numerical techniques to simulate quantum systems described by tight-binding Hamiltonians on ultra-large lattices (billions of sites).
main_result: The methodology enables routine simulation of systems with billions of sites by keeping the memory footprint logarithmic in system size, overcoming limitations of explicit matrix methods.
method: It employs a unified tensor-network approach, mapping large real-space Hamiltonians onto Matrix Product Operators (MPOs) defined on an L-pseudospin chain. Key techniques include using quantics tensor cross interpolation and applying the Kernel Polynomial Method (KPM).
model_or_system: The models are general tight-binding Hamiltonians applicable to moiré superlattices, quasicrystals, and systems requiring non-Hermitian or correlated descriptions (e.g., Hubbard model, excitons). The system size $N$ can reach $10^{12}$ sites.
key_observables: Spectral functions ($A(\mathbf{k}, \omega)$), Local Density of States (LDOS), real-space topological invariants (Chern markers), and time evolution dynamics ($\langle x|ho(t)|xangle$).
important_parameters: System size $N$ up to billions of sites; bond dimension remaining modest (order of tens); energy $\omega \in (-1, 1)$ or complex energies for non-Hermitian analysis.
main_assumptions: The method relies on the tensor network compressibility of real-space structures and assumes that physical observables can be efficiently represented as MPOs/MPSs.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the mapping from real-space lattices to pseudospin chains, comparing memory scaling (MPO vs. full matrix), and showing the construction of spectral operators and topological markers using tensor contractions.
paper_structure: The paper details the mathematical framework by first establishing the MPO representation for Hamiltonians on various lattices (1D/2D) via shift tensors. It then outlines algorithms for calculating observables like spectral functions (via KPM), topological invariants, and time evolution (via von Neumann equation solvers).
why_interesting: This work provides a powerful computational toolkit that extends beyond standard DMRG or exact diagonalization limits, making it highly relevant for studying complex quantum materials where system sizes are the primary bottleneck.
